intro.t: The fourth Gospel: written so that you may believe.
b: John is different in texture from the other three Gospels: long conversations and speeches rather than short scenes, seven ‘signs’ rather than many miracles, and seven ‘I am’ sayings that echo God’s name in Exodus 3:14. John states his purpose near the end: ‘these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name’ (20:31).

The first half (chapters 1–12) shows Jesus revealing his glory to the world through signs and teaching. The second half (13–21) shows him with his disciples, then glorified in his death and resurrection. It is the deepest of the Gospels and, perhaps surprisingly, often the first one recommended to new readers: simple language, profound content.

What the Gospel says. The book does not name its author, but it claims to rest on an eyewitness, ‘the disciple whom Jesus loved’: ‘This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down’ (21:20–24). This disciple was at the Last Supper, the cross and the empty tomb.

The early church. Irenaeus (about AD 180) wrote that John, the disciple who leaned on Jesus’ breast, ‘did himself publish a Gospel during his residence at Ephesus in Asia’. Clement of Alexandria and others repeat this. But a remark by Papias (early 2nd century) mentions both the apostle John and an ‘elder John’, and some scholars think the elder, not the apostle, was the author.

Where scholars stand. Opinion is divided. Many critical scholars think the Gospel came from a circle of the beloved disciple’s followers (a ‘Johannine community’), perhaps with several stages of writing. The traditional view, defended by scholars such as B. F. Westcott and J. B. Lightfoot and many since, is that the author was John the son of Zebedee. The case runs step by step: the writer was a Jew; a Jew of Palestine, who knows its places and customs closely; an eyewitness, who gives small details of time, number and place; one of the Twelve; and of the inner circle, which points to John, who is never named in this Gospel. The New Bible Dictionary concludes there are good grounds for a close link between the apostle and the writing, whether he wrote it himself or with a secretary or close disciple.

hist.t: When was it written, and is it reliable history?
b: Date. Most scholars date John in the AD 90s, the last of the four Gospels. Some, such as J. A. T. Robinson, argued for an earlier date. A small papyrus fragment of John 18 found in Egypt, known as P52 and now in the John Rylands Library in Manchester, is often called the earliest surviving piece of the New Testament. It has usually been dated to about AD 125–150, which would mean John was being copied far from Ephesus within decades. Some papyrologists, notably Brent Nongbri, argue that handwriting alone cannot date it so precisely, and that a later 2nd-century date is possible. Either way, the Gospel was known and used by the mid-2nd century.

History or theology? John is very different from Matthew, Mark and Luke: long speeches, few parables, much of the action in Jerusalem. For much of the 20th century many scholars treated it as theology rather than history. That has changed. Scholars increasingly recognise that John preserves independent historical traditions about Jesus, and archaeology has repeatedly confirmed the accuracy of his places: the pools of Bethesda (5:2) and Siloam (9:7), Jacob’s well (4:6) and the high priest Caiaphas (see the drop-downs below). John clearly shapes and interprets his material, and some of his wording may be his own reflection on Jesus’ words (some think 3:16–21 is John’s comment). But he insists he is giving testimony to real events: ‘his testimony is true’ (19:35; 21:24).

1.h: In the beginning was the Word
1.t: John opens with the first words of Genesis and then says three things: the Word was in the beginning, was with God, and was God. The second and third together rule out both that he is the Father and that he is a lesser being. Everything made was made through him.
Literally, pitched his tent among us — tabernacle language. The glory that filled the tent at Sinai is now in a person.

1.h: No one has ever seen God
1.t: The verse closes the prologue. The same Greek word for God appears twice in it without the article, and translations that render the two differently are making a decision the grammar does not require.

2.t: Roughly a hundred and twenty gallons of wine, at a wedding, from jars used for ceremonial washing. John calls the miracles signs rather than wonders because they point beyond themselves.

John places this at the start where the other Gospels place it at the end. Either there were two, or John has arranged his material thematically. He tells us plainly that the temple Jesus meant was his body.

3.t: The Greek phrase means both 'again' and 'from above', and Nicodemus hears only the first. Jesus' reply about the wind makes the point: the new birth is not something anyone manages.
'So' here means 'in this way' rather than 'so much' — the verse describes the manner of the love, which is the giving of the Son.
John the Baptist's last recorded words, and the cleanest statement of a right attitude to ministry in the New Testament.

4.t: Jesus crosses three barriers in one conversation — ethnic, gender, and moral. Note that he raises her situation directly rather than avoiding it, and that she is the first person in this Gospel he tells plainly that he is the Messiah.
The location of worship becomes irrelevant. God is spirit, and what he seeks is worshippers, which is an arresting way to put it.

5.t: John reports what the hearers understood, and Jesus does not correct them — he goes on to claim to do what the Father does, to give life, and to judge.
They study diligently and miss the point of the study. A warning aimed squarely at people who take the Bible seriously.

6.h: I am the bread of life
6.t: The first of the seven 'I am' statements with a predicate, spoken the day after the feeding and in a discourse about manna.

Our reading is the historic Reformed one: coming to Christ is something the Father enables rather than something we generate, and everyone he gives will in fact come. Other evangelicals read the drawing as a general influence that can be refused. Both sides hold Scripture to be true and are arguing about what it says here. We teach the first, and we say plainly that the second is held by Christians we respect. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

6.h: No one can come unless the Father draws him
6.t: Stated as an inability, not a reluctance. Verse 37 has already said that all the Father gives will come, and John places the two side by side without apology.
A hard saying, and most of the crowd leave. Peter's reply — to whom shall we go — is not enthusiasm but a reasoned conclusion that there is nowhere else.

7.t: Spoken on the last day of the feast when water was ceremonially poured. John explains that he meant the Spirit, not yet given.

8.t: Most modern Bibles set this passage apart with a note, and the BSB does. It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts of John, appears in different places in others, and its style differs from the rest of the Gospel. Many scholars think it records a real incident that circulated separately before being placed here. Either way, nothing taught elsewhere in Scripture depends on it, and the flagging is translators being honest rather than hiding something.

8.h: The truth will set you free
8.t: Usually quoted without its condition, which is abiding in his word. The freedom in view is from slavery to sin.
The response — picking up stones — shows how it was understood. The phrase reaches back to Exodus 3 and to the 'I am he' sayings of Isaiah.

9.t: A whole chapter on one healing, structured as a series of interrogations. The man's understanding grows through the chapter while the Pharisees' hardens. It ends with Jesus saying that those who claim to see are the guilty ones.

10.t: Against the background of Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's shepherds and says he will shepherd the flock himself.

10.h: I and the Father are one
10.t: The security of the sheep is stated twice — no one will snatch them from his hand, nor from the Father's — and then the two hands are identified. The crowd's reaction in verse 31 again shows what they heard.

11.h: I am the resurrection and the life
11.t: Said to a grieving woman before the miracle, and it reframes her hope from a distant event to a present person.
The shortest verse, and theologically among the heaviest: he is about to raise the man and he weeps anyway. Grief is not a failure of faith.

12.t: John quotes Isaiah 6 — the temple vision — and says Isaiah spoke about him. The subject through this passage does not change: the one not believed in, the one Isaiah spoke of, the one the rulers believed in.

13.t: The foot-washing is introduced by saying that Jesus knew the Father had given all things into his hands — and what he did with that knowledge was wash feet.
New in its measure: as I have loved you. The mark by which outsiders are to identify his disciples is how they treat each other.

14.h: The way, the truth and the life
14.t: Exclusive, and spoken as comfort to frightened men rather than as a slogan.
Philip's request and Jesus' reply. As direct a statement of his relation to the Father as the Gospel contains.
'Another of the same kind' — the Spirit is presented as a helper like Jesus himself, not a different order of thing.

15.t: Abiding is the whole instruction. Fruit is the result rather than the aim, and apart from him the yield is stated as nothing, not as less.

16.t: He convicts, guides into truth, and glorifies the Son. Verse 14 is decisive for how we pray: the Spirit's own work is to point away from himself and toward Christ.

17.t: Jesus prays for himself, for the Twelve, and then for everyone who would believe through their message — which includes the reader. The requested unity in verse 21 is patterned on the unity of Father and Son.

18.h: My kingdom is not of this world
18.t: Not that it has nothing to do with this world, but that its origin and method are elsewhere — which is why, he says, his servants are not fighting.

19.t: One word in Greek, tetelestai, used on receipts to mean 'paid in full'. It is a statement of completion, not defeat.
John stops the narrative to insist that he saw it. The detail matters to him because it establishes a real death against those who denied it.

20.t: Thomas addresses Jesus directly with both titles, and Jesus accepts it and pronounces a blessing on those who believe without seeing. It is the climax of the Gospel's argument.
John states his purpose: that you may believe, and believing have life. Everything selected was selected for that.

21.t: Peter denied three times and is asked three times. Jesus does not extract an apology; he gives him work to do. The restoration is public because the failure was.

1.ctx: John’s opening (1:1–18), often called the Prologue, deliberately echoes Genesis 1:1. ‘Word’ (Greek logos) spoke to Jews of God’s creative word (‘And God said…’) and of the wisdom of Proverbs 8, and to Greeks of the reason behind the universe. John goes far beyond both.
1.mean: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.’ Three statements. The Word already existed at the beginning: he was not created. The Word was ‘with God’, a distinct person in relationship with the Father. And ‘the Word was God’: he shares God’s own nature. ‘Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made.’ If everything that was made was made through him, he himself is not one of the things made. ‘In Him was life, and that life was the light of men. The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.’ The whole story of the Gospel, light opposed by darkness and victorious over it, is already here.
1.big: Jesus, the Word, existed before creation, is distinct from the Father, and is himself God, the Creator of all things.
1.diff: ‘The Word was God’ or ‘a god’? The Jehovah’s Witnesses’ New World Translation reads ‘the Word was a god’, arguing from the absence of the Greek article (‘the’) before ‘God’. Almost all translations, Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox, read ‘the Word was God’. Most Greek scholars explain that, in this word order, ‘God’ without the article describes what the Word is in nature, not ‘a’ member of a class of gods: John is saying the Word is truly God in nature, while distinct from the Father (‘with God’). Bruce Milne notes that if John had meant merely ‘divine’, Greek had a word for that (theios), which John does not use. And a lesser ‘god’ beside the one God would contradict the whole Bible’s insistence that there is only one God (Isaiah 44:6). The Gospel’s climax, Thomas’s ‘My Lord and my God!’ (20:28), confirms the reading.

1.ctx: John the Baptist was widely respected; some of his followers continued as a separate group long after his death (compare Acts 19:1–7). The Gospel makes clear he was a witness, not the Light.
1.mean: ‘There came a man who was sent from God. His name was John.’ He came ‘to testify about the Light, so that through him everyone might believe’. ‘The true Light, who gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.’ Then the tragedy: ‘He was in the world, and though the world was made through Him, the world did not recognize Him. He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him.’ The Creator came to his own creation, and to his own people Israel, and was turned away. ‘But to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God—children born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God.’ No one is a child of God by birth, family or effort. It is a new birth, and it comes from God.
1.big: Those who receive Jesus by believing in him are given the right to become God’s children, born of God.
1.diff: Verses 12–13 hold together two truths that Christians weigh differently. Reformed interpreters stress verse 13: the new birth is God’s work, ‘not of…the will of man’, so faith itself flows from God’s prior work. Arminian interpreters stress verse 12: God gives the right to become his children to all who receive and believe, and believing is a real human response made possible by grace. Both agree that no one can make themselves a child of God. See the key word Regeneration.

1.ctx: ‘Made His dwelling’ is literally ‘pitched his tent’ or ‘tabernacled’ (BSB footnote), recalling the tabernacle where God’s glory lived among Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 40:34).
1.mean: ‘The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.’ This is the heart of the Christian faith. The eternal Word did not just appear human, or visit a human; he became a real man, with a body and a human life. And in that human life, people saw God’s glory. John the Baptist testified that this one, who came after him, was before him. ‘From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.’ Moses asked to see God’s glory and could not (Exodus 33:18–23). ‘No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known.’ Jesus is the full explanation of God.
1.big: In Jesus, God himself became human and lived among us, and in him we see what God is like.
1.diff: This verse is the foundation of the church’s teaching on the incarnation and the two natures of Christ: one person, fully God and fully man (see the key word). In verse 18 some manuscripts read ‘the one and only Son’ and others ‘the only begotten God’ (BSB footnote); the BSB combines them as ‘the one and only Son, who is Himself God’. Either way, John calls the Son God at both ends of the Prologue (1:1, 18). ‘One and only’ (Greek monogenēs) means unique; the older translation ‘only begotten’ does not imply that the Son had a beginning.

1.h: The Mission of John the Baptist
1.ctx: Jewish leaders from Jerusalem sent a delegation to investigate John. Many were expecting Elijah to return before the Day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5) and a Prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15).
1.mean: Asked ‘Who are you?’, John answers with three denials: ‘I am not the Christ’, not Elijah, not the Prophet. He describes himself only by his task, in Isaiah’s words: ‘I am a voice of one calling in the wilderness, “Make straight the way for the Lord.”’ Isaiah 40:3 speaks of preparing the way for the LORD himself. When pressed about why he baptizes, he points away from himself to one already among them, ‘the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie’. Untying sandals was a slave’s job.
1.big: John the Baptist’s whole identity is to point away from himself to the coming Lord.
1.diff: Jesus elsewhere says John fulfilled the role of Elijah (Matthew 11:14). John denies being Elijah in person, which is what his questioners meant, while coming in Elijah’s spirit and power (Luke 1:17).

1.ctx: Lambs were central to Israel’s worship: the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the daily sacrifices, and the servant led ‘like a lamb to the slaughter’ (Isaiah 53:7).
1.mean: ‘Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!’ John identifies Jesus as the sacrifice God himself provides, and his reach is the whole world, not Israel only. He testifies that he saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove and remain on Jesus. This was the sign God had given him: ‘The man on whom you see the Spirit descend and rest is He who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.’ John’s verdict: ‘I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God.’
1.big: Jesus is the Lamb God provides to take away the world’s sin, and the Son of God who gives the Spirit.

1.ctx: ‘The tenth hour’ is about 4pm, counting from sunrise. Such small details are often seen as marks of an eyewitness.
1.mean: Two of John the Baptist’s disciples hear him say ‘Look, the Lamb of God!’ and follow Jesus. He asks, ‘What do you want?’ They ask where he is staying. ‘Come and see,’ he replies. One of them is Andrew. His first act is to find his brother Simon: ‘We have found the Messiah’. Jesus looks at Simon and gives him a new name, Cephas, which means Peter (‘rock’). The other disciple is not named; many think it was John himself, who never names himself in this Gospel.
1.big: Discipleship begins with Jesus’ invitation to ‘come and see’, and grows as one person brings another.

1.ctx: Nazareth was an insignificant village, never mentioned in the Old Testament.
1.mean: Jesus calls Philip: ‘Follow Me.’ Philip finds Nathanael: ‘We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law, the One the prophets foretold—Jesus of Nazareth’. Nathanael is sceptical: ‘Can anything good come from Nazareth?’ Philip does not argue: ‘Come and see.’ Jesus greets Nathanael as ‘a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit’, and reveals that he saw him under the fig tree before Philip called him. Nathanael is overwhelmed: ‘Rabbi…You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!’ Jesus promises greater things: ‘you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.’ This recalls Jacob’s ladder (Genesis 28:12). Jesus himself is the meeting place of heaven and earth.
1.big: Jesus is the true link between heaven and earth, the one the whole Old Testament pointed to.

2.ctx: A village wedding could last a week, and running out of wine would be a public disgrace for the family. The location of Cana is debated; many favour Khirbet Kana, about nine miles north of Nazareth.
2.mean: When the wine runs out, Jesus’ mother tells him. He replies, ‘Woman, what is that to you and to Me?…My hour has not yet come.’ ‘My hour’ runs through John and points to his death and glorification (12:23; 13:1). Mary simply tells the servants, ‘Do whatever He tells you.’ Six stone jars used for Jewish purification washing, each holding twenty to thirty gallons, are filled with water to the brim, and the water becomes wine, the best of the feast. ‘Jesus performed this, the first of His signs, at Cana in Galilee. He thus revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him.’ The jars for the old ritual washings are filled with the new wine of the kingdom; the prophets pictured the messianic age as abundant wine (Amos 9:13).
2.big: Jesus’ first sign reveals his glory and shows that he brings the abundant joy of God’s new age.
2.diff: ‘Woman’ was a polite form of address in that culture (Jesus uses it again from the cross, 19:26), though it marks a new distance: Mary cannot direct his mission. Christians differ on what this scene says about Mary. Catholic and Orthodox Christians see her as an intercessor who brings needs to her Son. Protestants typically emphasise her words ‘Do whatever He tells you’ as pointing away from herself to Christ. Christians also differ on whether the wine was alcoholic; the word normally means fermented wine, and the steward’s comment assumes it.

2.ctx: At Passover, worshippers needed approved animals and had to pay the temple tax in a particular coinage, so animal sellers and money changers operated in the large Court of the Gentiles.
2.mean: Jesus makes a whip of cords, drives out the animals and their sellers, and overturns the money changers’ tables: ‘How dare you turn My Father’s house into a marketplace!’ His disciples remember Psalm 69:9: ‘Zeal for Your house will consume Me.’ Challenged for a sign of his authority, he says: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again.’ They think he means the building, but ‘Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body’. God’s presence among his people would now be found in Jesus himself, and after his resurrection his disciples understood. Many believed because of his signs, but Jesus ‘did not entrust Himself to them, for He knew them all’: belief based only on miracles can be shallow.
2.big: Jesus himself is the new temple, the place where God meets his people, raised up after three days.
2.diff: Matthew, Mark and Luke place a temple cleansing in Jesus’ final week; John places one at the start of his ministry. Some scholars think there were two cleansings, one at the beginning and one at the end. Others think John has placed the single event early for theological reasons. Both views are held by scholars who accept the accuracy of the Gospels.

b: Josephus says Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple ‘in the eighteenth year of his reign’, usually reckoned as 20/19 BC. Forty-six years later brings us to about AD 27/28, which fits well with the start of Jesus’ ministry as dated by Luke 3:1 (the fifteenth year of Tiberius). The work was still going on. Josephus says the temple was finally ‘finished’ in the early AD 60s, only a few years before the Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

3.ctx: Nicodemus was a Pharisee and a member of the ruling council. He reappears in 7:50 and 19:39, each time a little bolder.
3.mean: Nicodemus comes at night and starts with a compliment: ‘we know that You are a teacher who has come from God.’ Jesus goes straight to the heart: ‘no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.’ The Greek can mean ‘born again’ or ‘born from above’ (BSB footnote), and both are true. Nicodemus takes it literally. Jesus explains: ‘no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the Spirit. Flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit.’ Human nature can only reproduce human nature; spiritual life must come from God’s Spirit. And the Spirit is like the wind (the same word in Greek): free, unseen, known by its effects. Then Jesus speaks of how this new life comes: ‘Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.’ In Numbers 21, Israelites bitten by snakes were healed by looking at a bronze snake on a pole; now, those who look in faith to the crucified Christ are saved. ‘For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.’ God sent his Son ‘not…to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him’. But ‘whoever does not believe has already been condemned’, because ‘men loved the darkness rather than the Light’.
3.big: Everyone needs to be born again by God’s Spirit, and new life comes by believing in the Son God gave out of love for the world.
3.diff: ‘Water and the Spirit’ (verse 5) is read in several ways. (1) Baptism and the Spirit: Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran churches read ‘water’ as baptism; the Catholic Catechism says baptism ‘signifies and actually brings about the birth of water and the Spirit’ (1215). Wesley also related it to baptism as the ‘outward sign and means’ of the new birth, ‘wherever baptism can be had’. (2) The Spirit’s cleansing: Calvin argued that ‘water’ and ‘Spirit’ describe one thing, the Spirit’s cleansing work (compare Ezekiel 36:25–27): ‘I cannot bring myself to believe that Christ speaks of baptism’. (3) Natural birth and spiritual birth, though this is less common. All agree that the new birth is the Spirit’s work. ‘The world’ in verse 16: Wesley read it as ‘all men under heaven’; Reformed readers agree that God’s love reaches the whole sinful world and the gospel is to be offered to all, while holding that God saves effectually those he chose (see the key word Election).

3.ctx: For a time John the Baptist and Jesus’ disciples were both baptizing, and John’s followers were troubled that the crowds were going to Jesus.
3.mean: John answers his disciples with humility: ‘A man can receive only what is given him from heaven.’ He is ‘the friend of the bridegroom’, the best man, whose joy is to hear the bridegroom’s voice. ‘He must increase; I must decrease.’ Verses 31–36 then describe Jesus as the one ‘from above’, who speaks the words of God and to whom ‘God gives the Spirit without limit’. ‘The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in His hands.’ The chapter ends with a stark choice: ‘Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Whoever rejects the Son will not see life. Instead, the wrath of God remains on him.’
3.big: John the Baptist rejoices to fade so that Jesus may be seen, because life or wrath depends on how people respond to the Son.
3.diff: Translators disagree where John the Baptist’s words end and the Gospel writer’s comments begin (after verse 30, or at verse 36). It makes little difference to the meaning.

4.ctx: Jews and Samaritans had been hostile for centuries. Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses and worshipped on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem. ‘The sixth hour’ is about noon, the heat of the day.
4.mean: Jesus, ‘weary from His journey’, sits by Jacob’s well and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, crossing barriers of race, religion and sex. He offers her ‘living water’ (fresh, flowing water, and also life itself): ‘whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst. Indeed, the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.’ When she asks for it, he gently exposes her life: she has had five husbands, and the man she now lives with is not her husband. She changes the subject to the old dispute about where to worship. Jesus answers that the place no longer matters: ‘a time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth’. ‘God is Spirit’. She says, ‘I know that Messiah…is coming.’ Jesus replies, ‘I who speak to you am He.’ It is one of his clearest statements anywhere in the Gospels that he is the Messiah, made to a Samaritan woman with a broken past.
4.big: Jesus offers the living water of eternal life to anyone, however far outside or broken they are, and calls for worship in spirit and truth.
4.diff: ‘Salvation is from the Jews’ (verse 22) keeps both truths together: God worked through Israel, and the Messiah is a Jew, yet he is ‘the Savior of the world’ (verse 42).

b: Jacob’s well is one of the few places in the Gospels whose location is not in dispute. It lies at the foot of Mount Gerizim (the Samaritans’ holy mountain, which the woman points to in 4:20), near ancient Shechem and the village of Askar, usually identified with Sychar. A pilgrim from Bordeaux recorded it in AD 333, a church was built over it in the 4th century, and the well, which is very deep (compare 4:11), can still be visited today beneath a Greek Orthodox church.

4.ctx: Rabbis generally avoided talking with women in public, which explains the disciples’ surprise.
4.mean: The disciples are surprised to find Jesus talking with a woman, but say nothing. She leaves her water jar, goes back into town and says, ‘Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?’ Meanwhile, the disciples urge Jesus to eat. He says, ‘My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.’ ‘Lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are ripe for harvest.’ As he speaks, Samaritans are coming out of the town towards him: the harvest is in front of them.
4.big: Doing the Father’s will is what sustains Jesus, and the harvest of people ready for the gospel is already here.

4.ctx: The woman’s testimony brings her whole town to Jesus.
4.mean: ‘Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in Jesus because of the woman’s testimony’. They ask him to stay, and he stays two days. Then many more believe because of his own words. ‘We now believe not only because of your words; we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this man truly is the Savior of the world.’
4.big: Faith that begins through someone else’s testimony becomes personal through hearing Jesus for oneself.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

4.ctx: A royal official probably served Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. Capernaum was about twenty miles from Cana and lower down, by the lake. ‘The seventh hour’ is about 1pm.
4.mean: The official begs Jesus to come down and heal his dying son. Jesus first challenges a faith that depends on spectacle: ‘Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will never believe.’ The father persists. ‘“Go,” said Jesus. “Your son will live.” The man took Jesus at His word and departed.’ On the way home his servants meet him: the boy is alive. The fever left him at the very hour Jesus spoke. ‘And he and all his household believed.’ It is ‘the second sign’.
4.big: Jesus’ word has power at a distance, and real faith takes him at his word before it sees the result.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

5.ctx: The pool lay just north of the temple, near the Sheep Gate (see the drop-down).
5.mean: Many sick people lay in the colonnades around the pool. One man had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks him, ‘Do you want to get well?’ The man explains that he has no one to help him into the water when it is stirred. Jesus says, ‘Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.’ Immediately he is healed. But it is the Sabbath, and the authorities object that carrying a mat is work. Later Jesus finds the man in the temple: ‘See, you have been made well. Stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you.’
5.big: Jesus heals by his word alone a man no one else could help, and calls him to a changed life.
5.diff: Verse 4 (an angel stirring the water) is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is omitted from the BSB text (it appears in a footnote). Jesus’ warning in verse 14 does not mean all illness is caused by personal sin (see 9:3), but that sin is more dangerous than sickness.

b: John describes a pool ‘near the Sheep Gate’ with ‘five covered colonnades’. In the 19th century, excavations beside the Church of St Anne, just north of the temple area, uncovered a large twin pool. Ancient writers, including Eusebius and a 4th-century pilgrim, describe twin pools here, and a Dead Sea Scroll (the Copper Scroll) mentions a twin pool by a similar name. Many scholars, following Joachim Jeremias, identify this with John’s pool: colonnades on the four sides and a fifth across the wall dividing the two pools would explain the five.

The identification is widely accepted, though not certain; older writers proposed other pools. The name also varies in the manuscripts (Bethesda, Bethzatha, Bethsaida). Verse 4, about an angel stirring the water, is missing from the earliest manuscripts and is probably a later explanation of the popular belief mentioned in verse 7.

5.ctx: Jewish teachers agreed that God himself kept working on the Sabbath: sustaining the world, giving life and judging.
5.mean: Jesus answers the charge of Sabbath-breaking: ‘To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working.’ His opponents understand exactly what he is claiming: ‘He was even calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.’ Jesus does not correct them. He explains: the Son does nothing on his own, but does whatever the Father does. Two things belong to God alone, and the Father has given both to the Son: giving life (‘the Son gives life to whom He wishes’) and judgment (‘the Father…has assigned all judgment to the Son’). The purpose: ‘so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.’ ‘Whoever hears My word and believes Him who sent Me has eternal life and will not come under judgment. Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life.’ And a day is coming when all in their graves will hear his voice and come out to resurrection.
5.big: Jesus shares the Father’s work of giving life and judging, and is to be honoured just as the Father is honoured.
5.diff: ‘The Son can do nothing by Himself’ (verse 19) is sometimes used to argue that the Son is lesser than God. The historic Christian reading is that it describes the perfect unity of the Father and Son’s action, not inferiority of nature: whatever the Father does, the Son also does, and he is to receive the same honour (verse 23).

5.ctx: Jewish law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15).
5.mean: Jesus lists his witnesses. John the Baptist testified to the truth; he ‘was a lamp that burned and gave light’. Greater still are ‘the works that the Father has given Me to accomplish’. And ‘the Father who sent Me has Himself testified about Me.’
5.big: Jesus’ claims are backed by John the Baptist, by his works, and by the Father himself.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

5.ctx: Jesus addresses religious leaders who studied the Scriptures intensely.
5.mean: ‘You pore over the Scriptures because you presume that by them you possess eternal life. These are the very words that testify about Me, yet you refuse to come to Me to have life.’ It is possible to study the Bible carefully and miss its point. The problem is not lack of knowledge but desire: ‘you accept glory from one another, yet do not seek the glory that comes from the only God’. ‘If you had believed Moses, you would believe Me, because he wrote about Me.’
5.big: The whole Old Testament points to Jesus, and studying it without coming to him misses its purpose.

6.h: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
6.ctx: The only miracle (apart from the resurrection) recorded in all four Gospels. It was near Passover, when Jews remembered the exodus and the manna in the wilderness.
6.mean: A large crowd follows Jesus. He tests Philip: ‘Where can we buy bread for these people to eat?’ Philip calculates that two hundred denarii, about eight months’ wages, would not be enough. Andrew finds ‘a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish’, the food of the poor. Jesus gives thanks and distributes as much as they want, and twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered. The people conclude, ‘Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world’, the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15). But they want to make him king by force, and Jesus withdraws. He will not be the kind of king they want.
6.big: Jesus provides abundantly from almost nothing, but refuses to be made the kind of king the crowd wants.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

6.ctx: The Sea of Galilee is subject to sudden strong winds funnelled through the surrounding hills.
6.mean: The disciples are rowing across the lake at night against a strong wind. After about three or four miles, they see Jesus walking on the water and are terrified. He says: ‘It is I; do not be afraid.’ The Greek is literally ‘I am’. In the Old Testament it is God who ‘treads on the waves of the sea’ (Job 9:8). They take him into the boat, and at once they reach the shore.
6.big: Jesus is Lord over the forces of nature, and his presence turns fear into safety.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

6.ctx: The crowd finds Jesus in the synagogue at Capernaum (verse 59). They ask for a sign like the manna Moses gave.
6.mean: Jesus tells the crowd they are looking for him because they ate their fill, not because they understood the sign. ‘Do not work for food that perishes, but for food that endures to eternal life’. What must they do? ‘The work of God is this: to believe in the One He has sent.’ Then the first ‘I am’ saying: ‘I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst.’ Manna kept Israel alive for a day; Jesus gives life forever. Then he speaks of God’s purpose: ‘Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me, and the one who comes to Me I will never drive away.’ ‘I shall lose none of those He has given Me, but raise them up at the last day.’ ‘No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him’. Then the language becomes startling: ‘this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh.’ ‘Unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you.’ ‘Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood remains in Me, and I in him.’ Life comes through his death, and through a union with him as close as eating.
6.big: Jesus is the bread of life, given in his death, and all who come to him in faith are kept by him and raised at the last day.
6.diff:
The Father’s drawing (verses 37–44). Reformed: those the Father gives to the Son will certainly come, and the Father’s drawing is effective. Calvin calls it ‘a powerful impulse of the Holy Spirit, which makes men willing who formerly were unwilling’, not violent or forced. Arminian (Wesleyan): God draws everyone, but his drawing can be refused. Wesley: ‘by the strong and sweet, yet still resistible, motions of his heavenly grace’. Both agree that no one comes to Christ without God taking the first step, and that whoever does come is never turned away.

Eating his flesh (verses 51–58). Catholic and Orthodox Christians see here the Eucharist: the Catechism quotes verse 53 in teaching that believers must receive the body and blood of Christ (1384). Lutherans also link it with the real presence of Christ in the Lord’s Supper. Reformed and other Protestants read it mainly as a vivid picture of faith. Calvin said ‘this discourse does not relate to the Lord’s Supper’ but to the eating ‘which is done by faith only’, though he saw the Supper as a seal of it. Wesley: ‘Eating his flesh is only another expression for believing.’ Augustine, centuries earlier, put it memorably: ‘Believe, and you have eaten already.’ Many interpreters hold both together: Jesus speaks of believing in his sacrificial death, and the Lord’s Supper is the meal in which that faith is expressed and fed.

6.ctx: The teaching was given in the synagogue at Capernaum.
6.mean: Many of his disciples say, ‘This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?’ Jesus asks what they will think if they see the Son of Man ascend to where he was before. Then he explains: ‘The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words I have spoken to you are spirit and they are life.’ He is not speaking of literally eating his flesh in a crude, physical sense; his words are received by the Spirit and by faith. Jesus knew from the beginning who did not believe. ‘No one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him.’ ‘From that time on many of His disciples turned back and no longer walked with Him.’
6.big: Jesus’ words are spirit and life, but they divide people, and many who followed for a while walk away.
6.diff: Verse 63 is read differently. Protestants often see it as confirming that Jesus spoke of spiritual eating by faith. Catholics and Lutherans read ‘the flesh profits nothing’ as referring to merely human understanding, not to Christ’s flesh, which gives life.

6.ctx: The crowds have gone; only the Twelve remain.
6.mean: Jesus asks the Twelve, ‘Do you want to leave too?’ Peter answers for them all: ‘Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life. We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God.’ Peter does not claim to understand everything. He simply knows there is nowhere else to go. Yet Jesus warns that even among the Twelve, ‘one of you is a devil!’, meaning Judas.
6.big: Real faith may not understand everything, but knows that Jesus alone has the words of eternal life.

7.ctx: The Feast of Tabernacles (Booths) in the autumn celebrated the harvest and remembered Israel’s years in the wilderness. Pilgrims lived in shelters made of branches for a week.
7.mean: Jesus’ brothers urge him to go to Judea and show himself publicly: ‘For even His own brothers did not believe in Him.’ Jesus replies that his time has not yet come. He goes up later, privately, and halfway through the feast begins teaching in the temple courts. People are amazed at his learning without formal training. He answers: ‘My teaching is not My own…It comes from Him who sent Me. If anyone desires to do His will, he will know whether My teaching is from God’. Truth about Jesus is recognised by those willing to obey God. He defends his Sabbath healing: if a boy can be circumcised on the Sabbath, why be angry that he made a whole man well? ‘Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly.’
7.big: Those who truly want to do God’s will recognise that Jesus’ teaching comes from God.
7.diff: On who Jesus’ ‘brothers’ were, Christians hold three views. Most Protestants take them as younger children of Mary and Joseph. Eastern Orthodox tradition sees them as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage. Catholic teaching holds that they were close relatives, not children of Mary (Catechism 500). See also the note on James 1:1.

7.ctx: Some Jews believed the Messiah’s origins would be mysterious and hidden until he appeared.
7.mean: People in Jerusalem wonder: the authorities are not stopping him. Could they think he is the Christ? But they object, ‘we know where this man is from.’ Jesus answers that they know his earthly origin, but not the One who sent him: ‘I know Him, because I am from Him and He sent Me.’ They try to seize him, ‘but no one laid a hand on Him, because His hour had not yet come.’ Many believe. The authorities send officers to arrest him. Jesus says he is going where they cannot come.
7.big: Jesus’ true origin is from God, and no one can touch him before God’s appointed hour.

7.ctx: According to the Mishnah (a Jewish law code compiled about AD 200), during Tabernacles a priest filled a golden jug with water from the Pool of Siloam and poured it out at the altar, a ceremony connected with prayer for rain.
7.mean: ‘On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood up and called out in a loud voice, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink. Whoever believes in Me, as the Scripture has said: ‘Streams of living water will flow from within him.’”’ John explains: ‘He was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were later to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.’ The water ceremony looked back and forward; Jesus says he is its fulfilment.
7.big: Jesus invites the thirsty to come to him and promises the Spirit as a river of life within.
7.diff: ‘From within him’ could refer to the believer, or to Christ himself as the source of living water. No single Old Testament verse matches the quotation; it probably gathers passages such as Isaiah 58:11, Ezekiel 47 and Zechariah 14:8.

7.ctx: The crowd’s debate shows what different groups expected.
7.mean: Some say he is the Prophet, others the Christ. Others object: ‘How can the Christ come from Galilee? Doesn’t the Scripture say that the Christ will come from the line of David and from Bethlehem?’ John’s readers know the irony: Jesus was in fact born in Bethlehem and of David’s line (Matthew 2; Luke 2). ‘So there was division in the crowd because of Jesus.’
7.big: Jesus divides people, and some reject him on the basis of half-knowledge.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

7.h: The Unbelief of the Jewish Leaders
7.ctx: Nicodemus (3:1) reappears, now speaking up a little in the council.
7.mean: The officers sent to arrest Jesus return empty-handed: ‘Never has anyone spoken like this man!’ The Pharisees scorn them and the crowd: ‘this crowd that does not know the law—they are under a curse.’ Nicodemus asks whether the law condemns someone without a hearing. They mock him too: ‘no prophet comes out of Galilee.’ (In fact Jonah came from Galilee, 2 Kings 14:25.)
7.big: Prejudice blinds the leaders, while even their own officers sense that Jesus speaks like no one else.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

8.ctx: This passage (7:53–8:11) is a special case: see ‘Was it originally in John?’ below.
8.mean: The scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery and set a trap: ‘In the Law Moses commanded us to stone such a woman. So what do You say?’ If Jesus says ‘let her go’, he contradicts Moses; if ‘stone her’, he defies Roman rule, under which the Jewish authorities could not carry out executions (compare 18:31), and loses his reputation for mercy. Jesus writes on the ground, then says: ‘Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her.’ One by one, starting with the oldest, they leave. Jesus is left with the woman. ‘Has no one condemned you?’ ‘No one, Lord.’ ‘Then neither do I condemn you…Now go and sin no more.’ Mercy and holiness meet: he does not condemn her, and he does not excuse her sin.
8.big: Jesus exposes the self-righteous, refuses to condemn the sinner, and calls her to a new life.
8.diff: Was it originally in John? The passage is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts of John. Where it does appear, it is found in different places in different manuscripts, and its style differs from John’s. Most scholars, including conservative evangelicals, conclude it was not part of John’s original Gospel. Many also think it is a genuine early story about Jesus, preserved by the church and later placed here. Most modern Bibles keep it in brackets with a note. Churches differ on whether to preach from it as Scripture; many do so with an explanation. What Jesus wrote on the ground is unknown; guesses are only guesses.

src.l: ‘John, Gospel of’, ‘Bethesda’ (D. F. Payne), New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

8.h: Jesus the Light of the World
8.ctx: According to the Mishnah, during Tabernacles great golden lampstands were lit in the temple’s Court of the Women, so bright that ‘there was not a courtyard in Jerusalem that was not illuminated’. Jesus is speaking ‘near the treasury’ (verse 20), in that court.
8.mean: ‘I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.’ The Pharisees object that he is testifying about himself. Jesus answers that his testimony is true because he knows where he came from and where he is going, and that the Father also testifies about him, making the two witnesses the law requires. ‘If you knew Me, you would know My Father as well.’ Then a warning: ‘unless you believe that I am He, you will die in your sins.’ The Greek is simply ‘I am’.
8.big: Jesus is the light of the world, and to know him is to know the Father.

8.h: The Truth Will Set You Free
8.ctx: Addressed to Jews who had begun to believe in him, but whose faith was shallow (see verses 37–59).
8.mean: ‘If you continue in My word, you are truly My disciples. Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.’ They object that, as Abraham’s descendants, they have never been slaves. Jesus speaks of a deeper slavery: ‘everyone who sins is a slave to sin.’ ‘So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.’ Physical descent from Abraham is not enough; true children of Abraham do what Abraham did. Their wish to kill Jesus shows that their real father is the devil, ‘a murderer from the beginning’ and ‘the father of lies’. ‘Which of you can prove Me guilty of sin?’
8.big: Real freedom is freedom from sin, and only the Son can give it to those who continue in his word.
8.diff: Verse 44 is addressed to particular opponents who were trying to kill Jesus. It must never be used to condemn Jewish people as a whole, as it sadly has been in history. Jesus and all his first disciples were Jews.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

8.h: Before Abraham Was Born, I Am
8.ctx: In Exodus 3:14 God revealed his name to Moses: ‘I AM WHO I AM.’ The Greek Old Testament used ‘I am’ (egō eimi) for God’s self-description in Isaiah too (for example Isaiah 43:10).
8.mean: His opponents accuse Jesus of being demon-possessed. He replies: ‘if anyone keeps My word, he will never see death.’ They are outraged: Abraham and the prophets died. ‘Are You greater than our father Abraham?’ Jesus: ‘Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day. He saw it and was glad.’ ‘You are not yet fifty years old, and You have seen Abraham?’ Then: ‘Truly, truly, I tell you…before Abraham was born, I am!’ Not ‘I was’, but ‘I am’: timeless existence, using the name God gave himself. ‘At this, they picked up stones to throw at Him’, the penalty for blasphemy. They understood him perfectly.
8.big: Jesus claims not only to have existed before Abraham but to bear the eternal name of God.
8.diff: The Jehovah’s Witnesses’ New World Translation renders verse 58 ‘before Abraham came into existence, I have been’. Most scholars and translations reject this. The Greek is the present tense ‘I am’ (BSB footnote: ‘before Abraham was, I am!’), deliberately contrasted with Abraham ‘coming to be’. The crowd’s attempt to stone Jesus shows they heard a claim to deity, not merely a claim to be old.

9.h: Jesus Heals the Man Born Blind
9.ctx: Many assumed that serious illness was punishment for sin, even sin committed by parents. On the Pool of Siloam, see the drop-down.
9.mean: The disciples ask, ‘Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?’ Jesus rejects both options: ‘Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him.’ ‘While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.’ He makes mud with his saliva, puts it on the man’s eyes and tells him, ‘Go, wash in the Pool of Siloam’, which ‘means “Sent”’. ‘So the man went and washed, and came back seeing.’ His neighbours can hardly believe it is the same man. ‘I am the one,’ he keeps saying.
9.big: Suffering is not always punishment for sin; in Jesus’ hands it becomes an occasion to display God’s work.

b: The Pool of Siloam received water from the Gihon spring through Hezekiah’s tunnel (see 2 Kings 20:20). For centuries visitors were shown a small pool dating from the Byzantine period. In 2004, workers repairing a sewer pipe in the City of David uncovered two ancient steps. The archaeologist Eli Shukron, who was watching, alerted his colleague Ronny Reich, and they identified a much larger pool from the late Second Temple period, the time of Jesus, with broad flights of steps. Coins in the plaster show it was built no earlier than about 100 BC, and coins of the Jewish revolt show it was in use until about AD 70. It was probably used for ritual washing by pilgrims going up to the temple. The Israel Antiquities Authority and its partners have since been excavating it further.
John notes that Siloam ‘means “Sent”’. The man born blind is sent by the one whom the Father sent (9:4).

9.ctx: Making mud and healing were both counted as work, forbidden on the Sabbath in the Pharisees’ rules. Being ‘put out of the synagogue’ meant being cut off from community life.
9.mean: The Pharisees question the man; they are divided. They question his parents, who are afraid: ‘the Jews had already determined that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue.’ They call the man again: ‘We know that this man is a sinner.’ He gives one of the great answers in the Bible: ‘Whether He is a sinner I do not know. There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!’ Under pressure he grows bolder, even ironic: ‘Do you also want to become His disciples?’ ‘If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing.’ They throw him out.
9.big: Personal experience of Jesus’ work is a testimony no argument can overturn.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

9.ctx: The man has been thrown out by the religious authorities.
9.mean: Jesus finds him. ‘Do you believe in the Son of Man?’ ‘Who is He, Sir?…Tell me so that I may believe in Him.’ ‘You have already seen Him…He is the One speaking with you.’ ‘“Lord, I believe,” he said. And he worshiped Jesus.’ The man’s understanding has grown through the chapter: ‘the man they call Jesus’ (verse 11), ‘a prophet’ (verse 17), ‘from God’ (verse 33), and now ‘Lord’, worshipped. Then Jesus speaks of the deeper reversal: ‘For judgment I have come into this world, so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind.’ Those who claim to see, but refuse the light, remain guilty.
9.big: The man born blind comes to see and worship Jesus, while those who claim to see remain blind.

10.ctx: In the Old Testament God is Israel’s shepherd (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34), and he condemned Israel’s leaders as false shepherds who fed themselves rather than the flock (Ezekiel 34:1–10). This follows straight on from how the leaders treated the blind man.
10.mean: A true shepherd enters by the gate; the sheep know his voice, and he calls them by name. ‘I am the gate for the sheep…If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved.’ ‘The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness.’ Then: ‘I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.’ A hired hand runs from the wolf; the shepherd gives his life. ‘I know My sheep and My sheep know Me’. ‘I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well…Then there will be one flock and one shepherd.’ And his death is voluntary: ‘No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord. I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again.’
10.big: Jesus is the good shepherd who knows his sheep and freely lays down his life for them, and will gather one flock.
10.diff: ‘Other sheep’ (verse 16) are usually understood as Gentile believers, joined with Jewish believers in one flock. Reformed theology has often seen in ‘I lay down My life for the sheep’ support for the view that Christ died with a particular intention to save his people; Arminian theology reads it alongside 1:29 and 3:16 as consistent with his dying for all.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

10.h: Jesus at the Feast of Dedication
10.ctx: The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) in December celebrated the rededication of the temple in 164 BC, after the Maccabees threw out the idolatry of Antiochus IV (see the notes on Daniel 8 and 11). Solomon’s Colonnade was a covered walkway in the temple courts (compare Acts 3:11).
10.mean: ‘If You are the Christ, tell us plainly.’ Jesus says his works already testify, but they do not believe ‘because you are not My sheep’. ‘My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand. My Father who has given them to Me is greater than all. No one can snatch them out of My Father’s hand. I and the Father are one.’ They pick up stones again, ‘because You, who are a man, make Yourself out to be God.’ Jesus answers from Psalm 82:6, where God calls human judges ‘gods’: if Scripture can use that word of them, how is it blasphemy for the one the Father ‘sanctified and sent into the world’ to say ‘I am the Son of God’? ‘Believe the works themselves, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father.’
10.big: Jesus’ sheep are held secure in his hand and the Father’s, because he and the Father are one.
10.diff: Security (verses 28–29). These verses are a key text for the Reformed doctrine that true believers will persevere to the end (Westminster Confession 17.1): no one, including the believer himself, can snatch them out of Christ’s hand. Wesley read the promise as applying to those who keep following: they ‘shall never perish, provided they abide in my love’. Both agree that no outside power can tear a follower of Christ from him. ‘I and the Father are one’ (verse 30): ‘one’ is neuter in Greek, meaning one thing, not one person. Wesley summed up the historic reading: one ‘Not by consent of will only, but by unity of power, and consequently of nature’, which rules out both merging the Father and Son into one person and denying the Son’s full deity.

John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on John 10
Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

10.ctx: Jesus withdraws across the Jordan to where John the Baptist had first baptized (1:28).
10.mean: Many come to him there and say, ‘Although John never performed a sign, everything he said about this man was true.’ ‘And many in that place believed in Jesus.’ John the Baptist did no miracles, but his faithful witness bore fruit even after his death.
10.big: Faithful witness to Jesus bears fruit, even without miracles.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

11.ctx: Bethany was a village less than two miles from Jerusalem, on the far side of the Mount of Olives. Mary, Martha and Lazarus were close friends of Jesus.
11.mean: The sisters send word: ‘Lord, the one You love is sick.’ Jesus says the sickness is ‘for the glory of God’. Then John adds a surprising sequence: ‘Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So on hearing that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was for two days’. His delay was not lack of love but the shape his love took. Going back to Judea is dangerous; the disciples remind him of the attempts to stone him. Jesus speaks of Lazarus ‘sleeping’, then plainly: ‘Lazarus is dead, and for your sake I am glad I was not there, so that you may believe.’ Thomas, often remembered only for doubting, says bravely: ‘Let us also go, so that we may die with Him.’
11.big: Jesus’ delays are not a lack of love; he acts at the time that will show God’s glory most fully.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

11.ctx: Burial usually took place quickly. ‘Four days’ meant there could be no doubt that Lazarus was dead.
11.mean: Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Martha meets Jesus: ‘Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.’ Jesus: ‘Your brother will rise again.’ She believes in the resurrection at the last day. Jesus brings it into the present: ‘I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies. And everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die. Do you believe this?’ Martha’s answer is one of the great confessions of the Gospel: ‘Yes, Lord…I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world.’ Then Mary comes, weeping, with the same words. ‘When Jesus saw her weeping…He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled.’ ‘Jesus wept.’
11.big: Jesus is the resurrection and the life, and he weeps with those who weep.
11.diff: Jesus weeps, knowing he is about to raise Lazarus. It shows his full humanity, real grief and sympathy, held together with his divine power. ‘Deeply moved’ can also carry a sense of anger, perhaps at death itself and the misery it brings.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

11.ctx: Tombs were often caves or rock-cut chambers sealed with a stone. Bodies were wrapped in linen strips with spices.
11.mean: ‘Take away the stone,’ Jesus says. Martha protests: ‘Lord, by now he stinks’. ‘Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?’ Jesus prays aloud, thanking the Father for hearing him, for the sake of those listening. Then he calls out in a loud voice, ‘Lazarus, come out!’ ‘The man who had been dead came out with his hands and feet bound in strips of linen, and his face wrapped in a cloth.’ ‘Unwrap him and let him go.’ This is the seventh and greatest sign in John’s Gospel before the resurrection: a man four days dead called back to life by Jesus’ word.
11.big: Jesus’ word has power over death itself, a sign of the resurrection to come.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 1 (chs. 1–11), CCEL

11.ctx: The council (Sanhedrin) was the Jewish ruling body in Jerusalem, led by the high priest under Roman oversight. On Caiaphas, see the drop-down.
11.mean: Many believe, but some report to the Pharisees. The council meets: ‘If we let Him go on like this, everyone will believe in Him, and then the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.’ Caiaphas, the high priest, gives a cynical political answer: ‘it is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish.’ John sees a deeper meaning Caiaphas never intended: ‘he was prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one.’ ‘So from that day on they plotted to kill Him.’ The greatest sign of life leads directly to the plot to kill the giver of life.
11.big: God turns even the scheming of Jesus’ enemies into a statement of the gospel: one man dying for the people.

b: Caiaphas is well known outside the Gospels. Josephus calls him ‘Joseph Caiaphas’ and records his appointment under the governor Valerius Gratus. He held office from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long time, covering the whole of Pilate’s governorship.

The Caiaphas ossuary (Widely accepted). In 1990 builders accidentally uncovered a family tomb in modern Jerusalem, outside the ancient city. One finely decorated bone box (ossuary) is inscribed ‘Joseph, son of Caiaphas’ and held the bones of a man of about sixty. Many scholars think it is the high priest’s. It cannot be certain, because Joseph was a common name and the inscription does not mention the high priesthood.
