‘Caiaphas’ (Archaeological Evidence), Lexham Bible Dictionary

12.ctx: Six days before the Passover, at Bethany. Nard was an expensive perfume; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages for a labourer (a denarius was a day’s pay, Matthew 20:2).
12.mean: At a dinner in Jesus’ honour, with Lazarus at the table, Mary takes about a pint of pure nard, anoints Jesus’ feet and wipes them with her hair. ‘And the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.’ Judas objects that it could have been sold for the poor. John explains his real motive: ‘he was a thief’, helping himself from the money bag. Jesus defends her: ‘She has kept this perfume in preparation for the day of My burial. The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me.’ Mary’s extravagant love sees what the disciples have missed: Jesus is about to die.
12.big: Extravagant devotion to Jesus is never wasted.
12.diff: ‘The poor you will always have with you’ echoes Deuteronomy 15:11, which continues: ‘that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land.’ It is not an excuse to neglect the poor.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

12.ctx: Lazarus himself had become living evidence of Jesus’ power.
12.mean: Crowds come to see not only Jesus but Lazarus. ‘So the chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus as well, for on account of him many of the Jews were deserting them and believing in Jesus.’ When the evidence is inconvenient, they plan to remove the evidence.
12.big: Hardened unbelief will try to destroy the evidence rather than accept it.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

12.ctx: Palm branches had greeted Jewish victors before: Simon Maccabeus entered Jerusalem’s citadel ‘with praise and palm branches’ (1 Maccabees 13:51). ‘Hosanna’ is Hebrew for ‘save, we pray’ or ‘save now’ (Psalm 118:25, BSB footnote).
12.mean: The crowd at the feast takes palm branches and goes out to meet Jesus: ‘Hosanna!’ ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!’ ‘Blessed is the King of Israel!’ Jesus finds a young donkey and sits on it, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9: ‘See, your King is coming, seated on the colt of a donkey.’ A conquering king rode a war horse; Jesus comes humbly, as a king of peace. The disciples understand only later, ‘after Jesus was glorified’. The Pharisees despair: ‘Look how the whole world has gone after Him!’
12.big: Jesus enters Jerusalem as the promised King, but a humble king of peace.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL
1 Maccabees 13:51 (World English Bible)

12.ctx: ‘Greeks’ were Gentiles who worshipped Israel’s God. Their coming signals that the world is indeed going after Jesus (verse 19).
12.mean: Some Greeks ask Philip: ‘Sir, we want to see Jesus.’ Jesus responds: ‘The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.’ The ‘hour’ that was ‘not yet’ (2:4; 7:30) has arrived. And his glory is his death: ‘unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.’ The same pattern applies to his followers: ‘Whoever loves his life will lose it, but whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.’ Jesus is troubled, but will not ask to be saved from this hour: ‘Father, glorify Your name!’ A voice from heaven answers. ‘Now judgment is upon this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out. And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself.’ ‘Lifted up’ means the cross, and also exaltation.
12.big: Jesus’ death is the hour of his glory, defeating Satan and drawing people of every nation to himself.
12.diff: ‘Draw everyone’ (verse 32). Calvin took ‘all’ to mean people of every kind, ‘the Church was to be gathered equally from among Gentiles and Jews’, which fits the coming of the Greeks. Wesley also read it as ‘Gentiles as well as Jews’, adding that those who follow his drawing cannot be held by Satan. Some read it as a universal drawing of every individual, which can be resisted. Compare the note on 6:44.

src.l: Calvin on John 12:27–33, CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on John 12

12.ctx: John’s summary of Jesus’ public ministry, closing the first half of the Gospel.
12.mean: ‘Although Jesus had performed so many signs in their presence, they still did not believe in Him.’ John explains this from Isaiah: ‘Lord, who has believed our message?’ (Isaiah 53:1), and ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts’ (Isaiah 6:10). ‘Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him.’ Some leaders believed but kept quiet, ‘For they loved praise from men more than praise from God.’ Jesus’ last public words: ‘whoever sees Me sees the One who sent Me.’ ‘I have not come to judge the world, but to save the world.’ But ‘The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.’
12.big: Rejecting Jesus is rejecting the God who sent him, and his own words will be the standard at the last day.
12.diff: Verse 41 refers to Isaiah’s vision of ‘the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted’ (Isaiah 6:1). John says the glory Isaiah saw was Jesus’ glory, another strong testimony to Christ’s deity. On God’s hardening (verse 40): Scripture holds together that people refuse to believe and are responsible (verse 37, 43), and that God judicially hardens those who persistently reject him. Christians differ on how these relate; compare the notes on Romans 9.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL
Bruce Milne, The Message of John, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)

13.ctx: Washing guests’ dusty feet was the job of the lowest servant. The Last Supper is described in John without the bread and cup, which the other Gospels record.
13.mean: ‘Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the very end.’ Knowing that the Father ‘had delivered all things into His hands’, Jesus gets up, takes off his outer garments, wraps a towel around his waist, and washes the disciples’ feet. Full authority and full humility in the same moment. Peter protests: ‘Never shall You wash my feet!’ Jesus: ‘Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me.’ Then Peter wants a full bath. Jesus explains that someone already bathed needs only his feet washed: the disciples are clean, ‘though not all of you’. Then the lesson: ‘if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another’s feet. I have set you an example’. ‘If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them.’
13.big: Jesus, who has all authority, takes the place of a servant, and calls his followers to serve one another the same way.
13.diff: Most churches read this as an example of humble service, not a ceremony to repeat. Some traditions practise foot-washing as an ordinance, and many churches do it on Maundy Thursday. The washing also pictures the deeper cleansing only Christ can give (‘Unless I wash you…’): once someone is ‘bathed’ (forgiven and made new), they still need daily cleansing from sin (compare 1 John 1:9).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

13.ctx: Guests reclined around a low table; the beloved disciple was next to Jesus.
13.mean: Jesus quotes Psalm 41:9: ‘The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me.’ He tells them beforehand ‘so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He.’ Troubled in spirit, he says, ‘one of you will betray Me.’ The beloved disciple, ‘reclining at His side’, asks who. Jesus gives the morsel to Judas, a last gesture of friendship. ‘And when Judas had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him.’ ‘What you are about to do, do quickly.’ ‘Judas went out into the night.’
13.big: Jesus knows his betrayer, offers him friendship to the last, and is in control of what happens.
13.diff: Judas’ betrayal raises the question of God’s plan and human responsibility. Scripture says it fulfilled what was written, that Satan entered him, and that Judas chose freely and was guilty (compare Luke 22:22). Christians hold all three together, though they explain the relationship differently.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

13.ctx: With Judas gone, Jesus speaks freely to the eleven. This begins the Farewell Discourse (13:31–16:33).
13.mean: ‘Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him.’ Jesus calls them ‘Little children’: he is going where they cannot yet come. Then: ‘A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another. By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.’ Love was commanded in the Old Testament (Leviticus 19:18). What is new is the measure, ‘as I have loved you’, to the point of death, and the effect: it marks out his disciples to the world.
13.big: Christ’s followers are to love one another as he loved them, and that love is their badge before the world.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

13.ctx: Peter, the leader of the Twelve, is confident in his own loyalty.
13.mean: Peter asks where Jesus is going. ‘Where I am going, you cannot follow Me now, but you will follow later.’ Peter insists: ‘I will lay down my life for You.’ Jesus: ‘Will you lay down your life for Me?…before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.’ Peter will in fact one day lay down his life (21:18–19), but not in his own strength, and not yet.
13.big: Self-confidence fails; Jesus knows our weakness and still promises we will follow him later.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

14.h: In My Father’s House Are Many Rooms
14.ctx: The disciples are dismayed: Jesus is leaving, one of them is a traitor, and Peter will deny him.
14.mean: ‘Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe in Me as well.’ Jesus asks for the same trust in him as in God. ‘In My Father’s house are many rooms.’ There is room for all who belong to him. ‘I am going there to prepare a place for you’. ‘And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am.’ The heart of heaven is being with Jesus.
14.big: Jesus goes to prepare a place for his people and will come back to take them to be with him.
14.diff: ‘Rooms’ (older translations ‘mansions’) means dwelling places. The picture is of a family home with room for everyone, not of private luxury.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

14.h: The Way, the Truth, and the Life
14.ctx: Thomas and Philip voice the disciples’ confusion.
14.mean: Thomas: ‘we do not know where You are going, so how can we know the way?’ Jesus: ‘I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.’ Jesus does not just show the way; he is the way. Philip: ‘Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.’ Jesus: ‘Philip, I have been with you all this time, and still you do not know Me? Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father.’ ‘I am in the Father and the Father is in Me’. Then a promise: ‘whoever believes in Me will also do the works that I am doing. He will do even greater things than these, because I am going to the Father.’ And: ‘I will do whatever you ask in My name’.
14.big: Jesus is the only way to the Father, and to see him is to see the Father.
14.diff: ‘No one comes to the Father except through Me.’ Historic Christianity of every tradition has taken this as teaching that salvation is through Christ alone. Christians differ on whether people who have never heard the gospel may be saved through Christ without knowing him explicitly. Catholic teaching holds that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the gospel but sincerely seek God ‘may achieve eternal salvation’ (Catechism 847), and some Protestants hold similar views. Most Reformed and many other evangelicals hold that salvation comes through hearing and believing the gospel (Romans 10:14–17). All agree there is no salvation apart from Christ. ‘Greater works’ is usually understood as the wider reach of the gospel through the church after Pentecost, not more spectacular miracles.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL
Bruce Milne, The Message of John, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)
Catechism of the Catholic Church 846–848 (salvation and the Church)

14.ctx: ‘Advocate’ translates the Greek paraklētos: one called alongside to help, a counsellor or defender (BSB footnote: Comforter, Helper, Counselor).
14.mean: ‘If you love Me, you will keep My commandments. And I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate to be with you forever—the Spirit of truth.’ ‘Another’ means another of the same kind: the Spirit will be to them what Jesus has been. The world cannot receive him, ‘But you do know Him, for He abides with you and will be in you.’ ‘I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.’ ‘Because I live, you also will live.’ Then a staggering promise: ‘If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word. My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our home with him.’ The Father, the Son and the Spirit all come to live with the believer.
14.big: Through the Spirit, the Father and the Son come to make their home with everyone who loves Jesus.
14.diff: ‘Another Advocate’ implies one like Jesus himself, a person, not an impersonal force. This matters in discussion with groups such as Jehovah’s Witnesses, who describe the holy spirit as God’s active force. John uses personal language of the Spirit throughout: he teaches, reminds, testifies, convicts and guides (14:26; 15:26; 16:8–13).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL
Bruce Milne, The Message of John, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)

14.ctx: ‘Peace’ (Hebrew shalom) was the ordinary greeting and farewell, but Jesus fills it with new meaning.
14.mean: ‘Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled; do not be afraid.’ ‘If you loved Me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.’ ‘The prince of this world is coming, and he has no claim on Me.’ Jesus goes to the cross not because Satan has any hold on him, but out of love for the Father and obedience to him. ‘Get up! Let us go on from here.’
14.big: Jesus gives a peace the world cannot give, rooted in his obedient love for the Father.
14.diff: ‘The Father is greater than I’ is cited by some, including Jehovah’s Witnesses, to deny Christ’s deity. The historic Christian reading is that Jesus speaks of his position as the incarnate Son on his mission, not of a lesser nature; elsewhere he says ‘I and the Father are one’ (10:30). Calvin says Christ is not showing ‘in what respect he differs in himself from the Father, but why he descended to us’.

src.l: Calvin on John 14:25–28, CCEL

15.ctx: Israel was often pictured as God’s vine or vineyard, usually one that failed to produce good fruit (Isaiah 5:1–7; Psalm 80:8–16).
15.mean: ‘I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard.’ Jesus is what Israel was meant to be. The Father ‘cuts off every branch in Me that bears no fruit, and every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes to make it even more fruitful.’ ‘Remain in Me, and I will remain in you.’ ‘I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing.’ A branch has no life of its own. ‘If anyone does not remain in Me, he is like a branch that is thrown away and withers.’ ‘This is to My Father’s glory, that you bear much fruit, proving yourselves to be My disciples.’
15.big: Fruitful Christian living comes only from staying connected to Jesus, the true vine.
15.diff: Verses 2 and 6 are debated in relation to whether true believers can finally fall away. Reformed interpreters generally read the fruitless branches as people outwardly attached to Christ (like Judas) but never truly united to him. Arminian interpreters read them as real branches, believers who stopped remaining in Christ and were lost. Both agree on the command: remain in him. See the key word Perseverance.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

15.ctx: The vine picture gives way to the language of friendship and love.
15.mean: ‘As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love.’ Remaining in his love means keeping his commands, as he kept the Father’s. His purpose is joy: ‘so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete.’ ‘This is My commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends.’ ‘No longer do I call you servants…But I have called you friends’, because he has shared with them everything the Father told him. ‘You did not choose Me, but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit—fruit that will remain’.
15.big: Jesus calls his followers friends, chosen by him, and commands them to love one another as he loved them.
15.diff: ‘You did not choose Me, but I chose you’ refers directly to Jesus’ calling of the apostles. Reformed theology also sees in it a principle of God’s gracious initiative in salvation generally; others limit it to choosing for service.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

15.ctx: ‘The world’ in John often means human society organised in rebellion against God.
15.mean: ‘If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first.’ ‘If you were of the world, it would love you as its own. Instead, the world hates you, because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world.’ ‘No servant is greater than his master. If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well’. Having seen his words and works, the world has no excuse. Then: ‘When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father—He will testify about Me. And you also must testify’.
15.big: Christ’s followers should expect the world’s hostility, and the Spirit and the disciples together bear witness to him.
15.diff: The filioque. Verse 26 is central to the oldest major disagreement between Eastern and Western Christianity. The Nicene Creed of 381 says the Spirit ‘proceeds from the Father’, echoing this verse. In the West, the words ‘and the Son’ (Latin filioque) were later added. Orthodox churches hold that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, citing this verse, and reject the addition; the Orthodox Catechism quotes John of Damascus that the Spirit is called ‘the Spirit of the Son’ but is not said to be ‘from the Son’. Catholic teaching keeps the filioque but acknowledges it was not in the Creed of 381, and says the Eastern phrase ‘from the Father through the Son’ and the Western one are a ‘legitimate complementarity’ (Catechism 246–248). Protestant churches generally kept the Western creed. Note that Jesus also says he will send the Spirit ‘from the Father’ (verse 26; 16:7).

Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed (381), in Schaff vol. 2

16.ctx: By the time John wrote, Jewish Christians were being excluded from synagogues, and Christians had been killed (Acts 7; 12:2).
16.mean: ‘I have told you these things so that you will not fall away. They will put you out of the synagogues. In fact, a time is coming when anyone who kills you will think he is offering a service to God.’ Religious persecution is often sincere. Jesus warns them in advance, ‘so that when their hour comes, you will remember that I told you’.
16.big: Jesus warns his followers in advance about persecution, so that it will not shake their faith.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

16.h: The Promise of the Holy Spirit
16.ctx: The disciples are grieving that Jesus is leaving.
16.mean: ‘it is for your benefit that I am going away. Unless I go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send Him to you.’ The Spirit will ‘convict the world in regard to sin and righteousness and judgment’: sin, because the world does not believe in Jesus; righteousness, because Jesus goes to the Father, vindicated; judgment, because ‘the prince of this world has been condemned’. For the disciples: ‘when the Spirit of truth comes, He will guide you into all truth. For He will not speak on His own…He will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine and disclosing it to you.’ ‘Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine.’
16.big: The Spirit convicts the world and guides Christ’s people into all truth, always pointing to Jesus.
16.diff: Verses 13–15 are often cited in describing the Spirit’s role: he points to Christ rather than drawing attention to himself. Many see in ‘guide you into all truth’ a promise fulfilled especially in the apostles’ teaching and the writing of the New Testament. Catholics and Orthodox also see in it the Spirit’s ongoing guidance of the church’s tradition.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

16.ctx: The disciples are puzzled by ‘a little while’.
16.mean: ‘In a little while you will see Me no more, and then after a little while you will see Me.’ Jesus explains with the picture of childbirth: ‘you will weep and wail while the world rejoices. You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy.’ A woman in labour forgets her pain when the child is born. ‘So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take away your joy.’ The cross will bring grief, the resurrection joy.
16.big: The sorrow of the cross gives way to a resurrection joy that no one can take away.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

16.mean: ‘Truly, truly, I tell you, whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you.’ ‘Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.’ ‘For the Father Himself loves you, because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God.’ The disciples think they finally understand. Jesus warns they will soon scatter and leave him alone. ‘Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me.’ Then the final word: ‘I have told you these things so that in Me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!’
16.big: In this world believers will have trouble, but in Christ, who has overcome the world, they have peace.
16.diff: ‘In My name’ means according to Christ’s character and purposes and on the basis of who he is, not a formula that guarantees any request.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

17.ctx: Often called Jesus’ ‘high priestly prayer’: he prays for himself, for his disciples, and for all future believers.
17.mean: ‘Father, the hour has come. Glorify Your Son, that Your Son may glorify You.’ The Father has given the Son authority over all people, ‘so that He may give eternal life to all those You have given Him. Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent.’ Eternal life is not only endless life but a relationship: knowing God. ‘I have glorified You on earth by accomplishing the work You gave Me to do. And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed.’
17.big: Eternal life is knowing the Father and the Son, and Jesus returns to the glory he shared with the Father before creation.
17.diff: ‘The only true God’ (verse 3) is cited by some to exclude the Son. The historic reading is that Jesus contrasts the one true God with false gods, while placing himself alongside the Father as the one whom to know is eternal life. In verse 5 he claims to have shared the Father’s glory before the world existed, and God shares his glory with no created being (Isaiah 42:8).

17.ctx: Jesus prays for the eleven, whom he is leaving in a hostile world.
17.mean: ‘I have revealed Your name to those You have given Me out of the world.’ ‘I ask on their behalf. I do not ask on behalf of the world, but on behalf of those You have given Me’. ‘Holy Father, protect them by Your name…so that they may be one as We are one.’ ‘Not one of them has been lost, except the son of destruction’, Judas. Jesus does not ask the Father to take them out of the world, ‘but that You keep them from the evil one’. ‘Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth.’ ‘As You sent Me into the world, I have also sent them into the world.’
17.big: Jesus prays that his disciples will be kept, made holy by God’s word, and sent into the world.

17.ctx: Jesus prays for every future believer, including every reader today.
17.mean: ‘I am not asking on behalf of them alone, but also on behalf of those who will believe in Me through their message, that all of them may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You. May they also be in Us, so that the world may believe that You sent Me.’ The unity of believers is modelled on the unity of the Father and Son, and it has a purpose: the world’s belief. ‘Father, I want those You have given Me to be with Me where I am, that they may see the glory You gave Me because You loved Me before the foundation of the world.’
17.big: Jesus prays for the unity of all believers, so that the world may believe, and that they may be with him to see his glory.
17.diff: Christians differ on what kind of unity Jesus prays for: a visible, institutional unity (a strong emphasis in Catholic and Orthodox thought and in the modern ecumenical movement) or a spiritual unity in truth and love that should show itself in visible fellowship (the usual evangelical emphasis). All agree that division among Christians damages their witness.

18.ctx: The garden across the Kidron Valley is Gethsemane on the Mount of Olives. The ‘band of soldiers’ was probably a detachment of Roman troops, with the temple police.
18.mean: Judas knows the place and comes with soldiers and officers, ‘carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons’. Jesus does not hide. ‘Jesus, knowing all that was coming upon Him, stepped forward and asked them, “Whom are you seeking?”’ ‘Jesus of Nazareth.’ ‘I am He.’ (Literally ‘I am’.) ‘When Jesus said, “I am He,” they drew back and fell to the ground.’ He protects his disciples: ‘let these men go.’ Peter draws a sword and cuts off the right ear of the high priest’s servant, Malchus. Jesus stops him: ‘Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?’
18.big: Jesus goes to his arrest in full control, protecting his disciples and willingly accepting the Father’s cup.

18.ctx: ‘Another disciple’ known to the high priest is often thought to be the beloved disciple himself.
18.mean: Peter and another disciple follow. The other disciple, known to the high priest, gets Peter into the courtyard. The servant girl at the door asks, ‘Aren’t you also one of this man’s disciples?’ ‘I am not,’ he answers. Inside, Jesus says ‘I am’; outside, Peter says ‘I am not’. Peter stands warming himself at a charcoal fire.
18.big: Under pressure even the boldest disciple can deny Jesus.

18.ctx: Annas had been high priest from about AD 6 to 15 and remained powerful; six members of his family, including his son-in-law Caiaphas, later held the office.
18.mean: Annas questions Jesus about his disciples and teaching. Jesus answers: ‘I have spoken openly to the world…I said nothing in secret. Why are you asking Me? Ask those who heard My message.’ An officer slaps him. Jesus responds calmly: ‘If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong. But if I spoke correctly, why did you strike Me?’ Annas sends him, still bound, to Caiaphas.
18.big: Jesus has nothing to hide, and calmly insists on justice even as he is mistreated.

18.ctx: The relative of Malchus had seen Peter with the sword in the garden.
18.mean: Asked again, Peter denies it: ‘I am not.’ Then a relative of the man whose ear Peter cut off asks, ‘Didn’t I see you with Him in the garden?’ ‘Peter denied it once more, and immediately a rooster crowed.’ Exactly as Jesus said. John tells it without comment; chapter 21 tells the rest of the story.
18.big: Jesus’ word about Peter’s failure comes true, but it is not the end of Peter’s story.

18.ctx: The Praetorium was the Roman governor’s headquarters (see the drop-downs on Pilate, on P52, and on the place of the trial at 19:1). Entering a Gentile house was thought to make a Jew ritually unclean for the Passover meal.
18.mean: The religious leaders will not enter the Praetorium, ‘to avoid being defiled’, while handing over an innocent man to death. Pilate asks the charge. ‘We are not permitted to execute anyone’. Inside, Pilate asks Jesus, ‘Are You the King of the Jews?’ Jesus answers: ‘My kingdom is not of this world; if it were, My servants would fight to prevent My arrest’. ‘For this reason I was born and have come into the world, to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to My voice.’ ‘What is truth?’ Pilate asks, and walks out without waiting for the answer. ‘I find no basis for a charge against Him.’ He offers to release him under a Passover custom, but the crowd shouts for Barabbas, ‘an insurrectionist’.
18.big: Jesus is a king, but his kingdom is not of this world; it advances by truth, not force.
18.diff: ‘My kingdom is not of this world’ describes the source and nature of his kingdom, not that it has nothing to do with this world. His kingdom does not come from the world’s power or use its methods.

b: Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36/37 and is one of the best-attested figures of the period. Josephus describes him bringing Roman standards bearing the emperor’s image into Jerusalem by night, backing down when crowds offered to die rather than see their law broken, and later using temple funds for an aqueduct and having protesters clubbed. Philo of Alexandria records another clash over shields in Jerusalem. The Roman historian Tacitus writes that ‘Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of the procurator Pontius Pilatus’.

The Pilate Stone. In 1961 Italian archaeologists excavating the theatre at Caesarea Maritima found a reused limestone block with a Latin inscription recording that Pilate dedicated a building in honour of the emperor Tiberius. It gives his title as ‘prefect of Judea’ and is now in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

The Gospels show Pilate under pressure and trying to avoid responsibility (19:12); Josephus and Philo show him harsh and provocative. Scholars suggest the pictures can be reconciled by Pilate’s position in Rome: his patron Sejanus was executed in AD 31, and a governor already accused of provoking the Jews could not afford a charge of disloyalty to Caesar (compare 19:12).

hist.t: P52: the oldest fragment of the New Testament
b: A scrap of papyrus about the size of a credit card, held in the John Rylands Library in Manchester, contains words from John 18:31–33 on one side and 18:37–38 on the other, Pilate questioning Jesus. Published in 1935 and known as P52, it is widely regarded as the oldest surviving fragment of any New Testament book. It has usually been dated to the first half of the 2nd century; some papyrologists argue that a somewhat later date is possible (see When was it written above). It comes from a codex (a book with pages), the format early Christians preferred.

19.ctx: Roman flogging was brutal and could itself kill. Pilate may have hoped it would satisfy the crowd.
19.mean: Pilate has Jesus flogged. The soldiers twist a crown of thorns, dress him in purple and mock him: ‘Hail, King of the Jews!’ Pilate brings him out: ‘Here is the man!’ The chief priests shout, ‘Crucify Him!’ They give their real charge: ‘He declared Himself to be the Son of God.’ Pilate is afraid. ‘Where are You from?’ Jesus is silent. ‘Do You not know that I have authority to release You and authority to crucify You?’ ‘You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above.’ Pilate tries to release him, but they press the political point: ‘If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar.’ Pilate sits on the judgment seat at ‘the Stone Pavement…Gabbatha’. ‘Here is your King!’ ‘We have no king but Caesar,’ reply the chief priests, a terrible statement from Israel’s leaders, whose true king was God.
19.big: Pilate’s power is real but borrowed; the true King stands silent while the leaders reject him for Caesar.
19.diff: Responsibility for Jesus’ death. John shows many responsible: Judas, the chief priests, Pilate, the crowd. The New Testament also teaches that Christ laid down his life freely (10:18) and that it was God’s plan (Acts 2:23), and that he died for the sins of all. John’s phrase ‘the Jews’ often means the Jerusalem authorities. Christian teaching of every tradition rejects blaming the Jewish people as a whole, a charge that caused terrible suffering in history.

b: John names the place of Pilate’s judgment seat as ‘the Stone Pavement, which in Hebrew is Gabbatha’. Christian tradition since the Middle Ages placed the trial at the Antonia Fortress beside the temple, and visitors are still shown a large paved area under the Sisters of Zion convent there. Archaeologists now date that pavement to the 2nd century AD, after Jesus’ time, when the Romans rebuilt the city.

The majority of scholars now think Pilate stayed at Herod’s former palace on the western hill when he came to Jerusalem. Josephus says a later governor, Florus, set up his judgment seat there. ‘Gabbatha’ probably means ‘high place’, which suits the palace on the highest part of the city. The exact spot is not certain.

19.ctx: Victims carried the crossbeam to the place of execution. A notice of the charge was often displayed. Golgotha means ‘Skull’; the Latin is ‘Calvary’.
19.mean: ‘Carrying His own cross, He went out to The Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha. There they crucified Him, and with Him two others, one on each side’. Pilate’s notice reads: JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS, in Hebrew, Latin and Greek, the languages of religion, government and culture. The chief priests want it changed; Pilate refuses: ‘What I have written, I have written.’ The soldiers divide his clothes and cast lots for his seamless tunic, fulfilling Psalm 22:18.
19.big: Jesus is crucified as ‘King of the Jews’, proclaimed, without meaning to, to the whole world.

b: Crucifixion was the Romans’ most shameful punishment, used for slaves and rebels. Ancient writers describe it often, but physical remains are rare, because bodies were usually left to decay or thrown away. In 1968, in a tomb at Giv’at ha-Mivtar in northern Jerusalem, archaeologists found an ossuary containing the bones of a crucified man from the 1st century AD, with an iron nail about 11.5 cm long still driven through his heel bone. It confirms that victims were nailed, as the Gospels imply (20:25), and that a crucified Jew could be given a proper family burial, as Jesus was.

19.ctx: Women followers stayed near the cross when most of the disciples had fled.
19.mean: Near the cross stand Jesus’ mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. Jesus sees his mother and the beloved disciple: ‘Woman, here is your son.’ ‘Here is your mother.’ ‘So from that hour, this disciple took her into his home.’ In his agony, Jesus provides for his mother. Then, ‘knowing that everything had now been accomplished, and to fulfill the Scripture, Jesus said, “I am thirsty.”’ He receives sour wine on hyssop, ‘He said, “It is finished.” And bowing His head, He yielded up His spirit.’ Not a cry of defeat but of completion: the work the Father gave him is done (17:4). And he gives up his spirit; it is not taken from him (10:18).
19.big: Jesus completes the work he came to do and gives up his life, finished, not defeated.
19.diff: Mary and the beloved disciple. Calvin saw here Jesus’ care for his mother, honouring her as a son through practical provision. Catholic teaching also sees a wider meaning: Mary’s spiritual motherhood of all believers, represented by the beloved disciple (Catechism 501 refers to this passage). Protestants generally read it as an act of family care, with the beloved disciple taking responsibility for her. ‘It is finished’ is one word in Greek (tetelestai), meaning ‘it has been completed’. Christians understand it as declaring that the work of atonement is complete; the Reformers drew from it that nothing needs to be added to Christ’s sacrifice.

19.ctx: Jewish law required bodies not to remain hanging overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), especially on a festival Sabbath. Breaking the legs hastened death.
19.mean: The soldiers break the legs of the two others, but find Jesus already dead. ‘Instead, one of the soldiers pierced His side with a spear, and immediately blood and water flowed out.’ Then a solemn statement of eyewitness: ‘The one who saw it has testified to this, and his testimony is true. He knows that he is telling the truth, so that you also may believe.’ Two Scriptures were fulfilled: ‘Not one of His bones will be broken’, said of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46), and ‘They will look on the One they have pierced’ (Zechariah 12:10).
19.big: Jesus really died, as an eyewitness solemnly testifies, and he died as the true Passover lamb.
19.diff: The blood and water have been read as evidence of real death (against the early heresy that Christ only seemed to have a body, and against modern ‘swoon’ theories), and symbolically, as pictures of the Lord’s Supper and baptism or of cleansing and life (compare 7:38). John’s own emphasis is on the eyewitness reality.

19.ctx: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus were both members of the ruling council. Seventy-five pounds of spices was a very large quantity, fit for a king.
19.mean: Joseph of Arimathea, ‘a disciple of Jesus (but secretly for fear of the Jews)’, asks Pilate for the body. Nicodemus, ‘who had previously come to Jesus at night’, brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes. Two secret disciples now come out into the open. They wrap the body in linen with the spices ‘according to the Jewish burial custom’. ‘Now there was a garden in the place where Jesus was crucified, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.’ Because the Sabbath was about to begin and the tomb was near, they placed Jesus there.
19.big: Jesus is honourably buried in a new tomb by two secret disciples who now step into the open.

hist.t: Where are Golgotha and the tomb? (19:41)
b: John says the crucifixion was ‘near the city’ (19:20), with a garden and a new tomb nearby. Two sites are shown today.

The Church of the Holy Sepulchre. In the 4th century the emperor Constantine built a church here over a site local Christians identified, under a temple Hadrian had built about AD 135. It is now inside the Old City walls, which once seemed to contradict the Gospels. But excavations, including Kathleen Kenyon’s in the 1960s, showed that in Jesus’ time the area was an old quarry outside the walls, with rock-cut tombs of the 1st century. Kenyon concluded that it had not been proved to be the site, but that it can be. Most archaeologists regard it as the most likely location.

The Garden Tomb. North of the Damascus Gate, identified by General Charles Gordon in 1883, it is a peaceful and moving place to visit. But excavations by Gabriel Barkay and Amos Kloner indicate that the tomb was first cut in the Iron Age (8th–7th centuries BC), so it would not have been a ‘new tomb in which no one had yet been laid’. Few archaeologists now think it was Jesus’ tomb.

20.ctx: ‘The first day of the week’ is Sunday, which Christians came to call the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10). Josephus records the Jewish rule of the time: ‘let not the testimony of women be admitted’. Yet all four Gospels name women as the first witnesses, which an inventor of the story would hardly have done.
20.mean: Early on Sunday, while still dark, Mary Magdalene finds the stone removed. She runs to Peter and the beloved disciple: ‘They have taken the Lord out of the tomb’. The two run to the tomb. The other disciple arrives first and sees the linen cloths. Peter goes in and sees the cloths lying there, and ‘The cloth that had been around Jesus’ head was rolled up, lying separate from the linen cloths.’ Then the other disciple goes in, ‘And he saw and believed.’ ‘For they still did not understand from the Scripture that Jesus had to rise from the dead.’
20.big: The empty tomb and the grave clothes left behind lead the beloved disciple to believe that Jesus has risen.
20.diff: The detail of the cloths is often noted as an eyewitness touch, and as a sign that the body was not stolen: grave robbers would not have unwrapped it and left the expensive linen and spices behind.

20.ctx: Mary Magdalene had been freed from seven demons by Jesus (Luke 8:2). She is the first witness of the risen Christ.
20.mean: Mary stays at the tomb weeping. She sees two angels, then turns and sees Jesus, but thinks he is the gardener. ‘Jesus said to her, “Mary.”’ At the sound of her name she knows him: ‘Rabboni!’ (Teacher). The good shepherd calls his sheep by name (10:3). ‘Do not cling to Me,’ Jesus says, ‘for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go and tell My brothers, “I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God.”’ The disciples are now his ‘brothers’, and his Father is their Father. Mary goes and announces: ‘I have seen the Lord!’
20.big: The risen Jesus calls Mary by name and sends her as the first witness of the resurrection.
20.diff: ‘My Father and your Father’ keeps a distinction: Jesus is Son by nature, believers are children by grace. He does not say ‘our Father’.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on John, vol. 2 (chs. 12–21), CCEL

20.ctx: The disciples are behind locked doors on the evening of the first Easter Sunday.
20.mean: ‘Jesus came and stood among them. “Peace be with you!”’ He shows them his hands and side, and ‘The disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.’ ‘As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you.’ He breathes on them and says, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven; if you withhold forgiveness from anyone, it is withheld.’ As God breathed life into Adam (Genesis 2:7), the risen Christ breathes new life into his church and sends it out.
20.big: The risen Jesus gives peace, sends his disciples as the Father sent him, and gives them the Spirit for their mission.
20.diff: Forgiving sins (verse 23). Catholic teaching sees here the institution of the sacrament of penance, through which priests absolve sins in Christ’s name (Catechism 1485). Protestants generally read it as the authority to declare forgiveness through the gospel: Calvin saw the apostles as ‘witnesses or heralds of this blessing, and not the authors of it’; Wesley as ‘A power of declaring with authority the Christian terms of pardon’ to those who repent and believe. Lutherans keep private confession and absolution as a valued practice. The Spirit given here and at Pentecost (Acts 2): views include a foretaste, a symbolic promise, or a distinct giving for the apostles’ commission.

20.ctx: Thomas (‘Didymus’ means twin) had earlier been willing to die with Jesus (11:16).
20.mean: Thomas was absent and refuses to believe without proof: ‘Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.’ Eight days later Jesus comes again, and offers him exactly the proof he asked for: ‘Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe.’ ‘Thomas replied, “My Lord and my God!”’ Jesus: ‘Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.’
20.big: The doubter becomes the one who makes the Gospel’s highest confession: Jesus is Lord and God.
20.diff: Thomas’s words are among the clearest direct confessions of Christ’s deity in the New Testament, and the climax of the Gospel that began ‘the Word was God’ (1:1). Some have suggested Thomas was only exclaiming in surprise, but Jesus accepts the words as a confession of faith, and a devout Jew would not use God’s name as an exclamation. Wesley noted that Thomas ‘confesses his Godhead, and that more explicitly than any other had yet done’.

20.ctx: These verses read like the original ending of the Gospel; chapter 21 forms an epilogue.
20.mean: ‘Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of His disciples, which are not written in this book. But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.’ John has been selective. His aim is not a complete biography but faith, and through faith, life.

21.h: Jesus Appears by the Sea of Tiberias
21.ctx: The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee. Most scholars think chapter 21 was added as an epilogue, probably by the author himself, though some think by his circle.
21.mean: Seven disciples go fishing at night and catch nothing. At dawn a figure on the shore tells them to cast the net on the right side. They cannot haul it in. The beloved disciple says, ‘It is the Lord!’ Peter jumps into the sea. On the shore there is ‘a charcoal fire there with fish on it, and some bread’. The catch is 153 large fish, ‘but even with so many, the net was not torn.’ ‘Come, have breakfast,’ Jesus says, and serves them himself.
21.big: The risen Jesus meets his disciples in their ordinary work, provides abundantly, and feeds them himself.
21.diff: The number 153 has been given many symbolic meanings (for example, the fullness of the nations to be gathered into the church). Many scholars think it is simply the remembered count of an eyewitness. The unbroken net may picture the unity of the church.

21.ctx: Peter had denied Jesus three times beside a charcoal fire (18:18); now, beside another charcoal fire, Jesus asks him three times.
21.mean: ‘Simon son of John, do you love Me more than these?’ ‘Yes, Lord…You know I love You.’ ‘Feed My lambs.’ A second time: ‘Shepherd My sheep.’ A third time, and Peter is hurt: ‘Lord, You know all things…You know I love You.’ ‘Feed My sheep.’ Three denials, three affirmations of love, three commissions. Jesus restores Peter publicly and gives him back his calling. Then he tells Peter how he will die: ‘when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go.’ ‘Follow Me.’
21.big: Jesus restores Peter after his failure, recommissions him to care for his flock, and calls him to follow to the end.
21.diff: Peter’s role. Catholic teaching sees here, with Matthew 16:18–19, Christ confirming Peter’s unique pastoral authority over the whole church (Catechism 553), handed on to his successors, the bishops of Rome. Orthodox and Protestant Christians generally read it as Peter’s personal restoration and recommissioning after his threefold denial, a charge that applies to all pastors (compare 1 Peter 5:1–4, where Peter calls himself a ‘fellow elder’). Two words for love. Jesus’ first two questions use agapaō, and Peter’s answers and the third question use phileō. Some build a contrast between them; many scholars think John uses the two words interchangeably here, as he does elsewhere.

b: Jesus says Peter will ‘stretch out your hands’, and John explains this indicated ‘the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God’. Early Christian tradition says Peter died as a martyr in Rome under Nero. Eusebius (4th century), citing Origen, records that Peter ‘was crucified head-downwards; for he had requested that he might suffer in this way’. The same history records that John lived on in Asia and died at Ephesus, which fits the rumour in verse 23 that he would not die.

21.ctx: The Gospel’s closing words identify its source.
21.mean: Peter sees the beloved disciple following and asks, ‘Lord, what about him?’ Jesus: ‘If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you? You follow Me!’ Every disciple has his own path; comparison is a distraction. A rumour spread that this disciple would not die, but Jesus did not say that. Then: ‘This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down. And we know that his testimony is true.’ ‘There are many more things that Jesus did. If all of them were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself would have space for the books that would be written.’
21.big: Each disciple must follow Jesus on his own path, and the Gospel rests on the true testimony of an eyewitness.
21.diff: The closing verses identify the beloved disciple as the Gospel’s source and witness. ‘We know’ suggests that others who knew him added their confirmation. Whether he wrote it all himself or others shaped the final form is discussed (see Who wrote John’s Gospel? above).
